chap: Chapter Two: Hands and a Road
snip: We had come up by then onto the first of the rough, where the walls give out and the wind owns the g
original: We had come up by then onto the first of the rough, where the walls give out and the wind owns the grass, and he swung his stick at the whole grey shoulder of it. "The high ground, all of it, the fell and the scrub above the tree line that runs back off the top of your hill farther than you'll walk in a day, that was nobody's and everybody's, sheep-run and weather; good ground enough in its way, and never once asked to be anything, for there's no man round here these forty years has had the money to ask it. Your man had the parish and the township set their marks to the whole of it, so it's yours now on the map, every stone and grouse of it. You've more untouched and unused land than one man could ever find a use for, on paper at least. You've not four hundred acres of it a plough has been over in ten years. Both of those are true, and you'd best learn to carry them in the one hand, for the valley will."

original: Cheap ground was cheap because it was poor. I had brought that out from the city with me, and one good field along a river was not going to shift it. So I was glad of the field, and went on, and Cael let me be glad.

original: "Four men had this," he said, as we went along the headland. "Four men and a parish. Now it's the one holding, and that's the first honest thing anybody's done to it since I was a lad."

chap: Chapter Two: Hands and a Road
snip: He stopped on the path and turned and looked at me, and there was nothing unkind in it. "Land wants
original: He stopped on the path and turned and looked at me, and there was nothing unkind in it. "Land wants two things, and it's the same two things everywhere I've ever heard of. It wants hands and it wants a road. You've bought yourself a deal of land with neither, and I'd not have you find that out in your own time and think we'd hidden it. That agent of his sat at my table three evenings running with a map and a pencil, and every evening the map got bigger and the pencil got sharper. I've sold land my whole life. I never once sold it to a man who wanted the ground his ground would need before his ground needed it, nor took the trouble to square the bits nobody else had ever thought worth the bother."

snip: I did not know him, the man in the story, though he wore my name. Emlyn. They had kept that much, an
original: I did not know him, the man in the story, though he wore my name. Emlyn. They had kept that much, and it is a strange thing to hear your own name walking about a taproom without you. They had made something else of me in those tales: a figure, a wonder, a man who walked through life already knowing its shape. He came up the valley meaning the tower, saw the whole of it standing behind his eyes on the first morning, raised it in a season, and the hill made no argument. He was never wrong about a footing, never sat a winter counting silver, never stood in the rain arguing with a wagon. The tellers are fond of such men: sure of themselves, untouched by anything, always the right word ready and never a wrong night lying behind them. The man they made is no one I ever met. I would not cross a room to shake his hand.
revised: I did not know him, the man in the story, though he used my name. Emlyn. They had, however, made something else of me in those tales: a figure, a wonder, a man who walked through life already knowing its shape. He came from nowhere to an abandoned valley with grand plans of a magic tower, saw the whole of it standing behind his eyes on the first morning, raised it in a season, and with no trouble. He was never wrong about a footing, never sat a winter counting silver, never stood in the rain arguing with a wagon. The tellers are fond of such men: sure of themselves, untouched by anything, always the right word ready and never a wrong night lying behind them. The man they made is no one I ever met.

snip: Not that the real one was any great prize. I will not sit here in my old age and pretend the man I w
original: Not that the real one was any great prize. I will not sit here in my old age and pretend the man I was then was wiser or gentler or one whit less a fool than the figure in the story. God knows I had a great deal more to learn than I had the sense to know I was missing, and I learned most of it the slow way, late, and at a cost to better people than myself. But he was a man, at least, and not a monument. If I leave one true thing behind me, I would sooner it were him than the bronze one the tellers have cast up in his place.
